rows.title: Finding the grievance officer
rows.body: An e-commerce entity must provide a grievance mechanism, appoint a grievance officer, and display the officer's name, contact details and designation on its platform.

rows.title: Complaint response timelines
rows.body: The grievance officer must acknowledge a consumer complaint within 48 hours and redress it within one month, measured from receipt of the complaint.

rows.title: Accepted refund requests
rows.body: An e-commerce entity must pay accepted refund requests within a reasonable period or the period prescribed under applicable law, following the requirements of the RBI or other competent authority. This provision does not specify a universal seven-day refund deadline.

rows.title: National Consumer Helpline
rows.body: NCH is a pre-litigation grievance mechanism. Consumers can contact it on 1915 or register through its portal. Its information page says reaching a logical conclusion may take up to 30 days; registering does not guarantee a remedy.
rows.source_name: National Consumer Helpline — About, questions 1, 3, 8 and 9

rows.title: If the helpline does not resolve it
rows.body: A consumer dissatisfied with the helpline outcome can approach the appropriate Consumer Commission. e-Jagriti is the government's portal for Consumer Commissions. Nivaran provides information at this step and does not prepare or file a Commission complaint.
rows.source_name: National Consumer Helpline — About; official e-Jagriti portal

rows.title: Tracing a processed refund
rows.body: In a published NCH case about a cancelled online train booking, the company advised the consumer to check the refund status with the card-issuing bank using the ARN it supplied. A reference supports tracing; it does not itself show that the account was credited. This example is practical tracing information, not a general legal deadline or a guarantee of recovery.
